source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: On MATH with a revision-finetuned PaLM 2-S*, N sequential revisions beat N parallel fresh samples at equal generation budget, with both verifier and majority-vote selection. The best mix of sequential and parallel depends on difficulty: easy questions favour pure revision, hard ones a balance.
numbers: Compute-optimal sequential/parallel split matched best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute (64 vs 256 samples). Sequential 'narrowly outperforms' parallel in Fig 6 right.
quote: easier questions benefit from purely sequential test-time compute, whereas harder questions often perform best with some ideal ratio
limits: Revision model was finetuned on MATH for revising; the base model's prompted revisions are weaker. Edits here are of the model's own attempts, not a retrieved case. A learned PRM/ORM verifier does the selecting. Math, one model family.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 1 only in part: at equal tokens, editing a prior attempt beats fresh samples on a reasoning task, but only with a trained reviser and a verifier, and the edited object is not a retrieved case. Use a mixed budget, not pure editing, on hard items.

source: Snell et al. (2024), section 6.1 revision failure rate
finding: A revision model that edits an answer already in context will often break a correct one. The authors had to add verifier or majority-vote selection over the revision chain to guard against it.
numbers: About 38% of correct answers were converted back to incorrect ones by the revision model with the naive approach (MATH, PaLM 2-S* revision model).
quote: around 38% of correct answers get converted back to incorrect ones
limits: Number is for a model trained only on incorrect-answer contexts (distribution shift at test time), so it may overstate the rate for a model trained or prompted differently. Cites Qu et al. for a similar finding.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: first measured break rate for editing a given solution, 38% unguarded. Our edit operator must keep the original and compare, never overwrite. Not a retrieved case, so the retrieved-case rate is still unmeasured.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Feedback quality drives edit gains. Specific actionable feedback beats generic feedback, which beats no feedback. One-vs-k test: refinement outputs were still preferred to all of k=4 plain samples.
numbers: Table 2: Code Optimization 27.5 / 26.0 / 24.8 (specific / generic / none); Sentiment Reversal 43.2 / 31.2 / 0; Acronym Generation 56.4 / 54.0 / 48.0. 1-vs-4 human preference test favoured Self-Refine.
limits: The 1-vs-k check is a human preference test, not accuracy, and is on open-ended tasks. Gains on math are nil (see d04). Same model gives feedback and edit, no external checker.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the diagnosis step is the active ingredient, not the edit. A separate diagnosis call earns its tokens when it is specific; generic 'improve it' does not. Equal-token comparison against diagnosis-free resampling was not run.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine, Table 9 and appendix on math reasoning
finding: On GSM8K-style math, self-feedback refinement gave no gain at any base level; only an oracle stop signal helped. Higher base accuracy left even less room.
numbers: Math Reasoning base to Self-Refine: GPT-3.5 64.1 to 64.1 (0); ChatGPT 74.8 to 75.0 (+0.2); GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1 (+0.2). With oracle feedback (GPT-3.5): 64.06 to 68.9 (+4.8).
limits: Math with program-of-thought answers; the authors blame the model being unable to spot errors in its own reasoning. Other tasks (dialogue, code readability) gained 8 to 30 points, so the shrink is task-specific.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: edit gain does not grow with model strength on reasoning and is already about zero near 93%. Plan to measure our edit step on frontier models and expect it to shrink where base accuracy is high. Gap 3: oracle signal, not the model, produced the gain.

source: Gou et al. (2023/2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Same revise loop with and without tool feedback. Without tools ('CRITIC w/o Tool') correction gives little or hurts; with search, code execution or a toxicity API it gives clear gains.
numbers: Open-domain QA table (first model block, EM): CoT 44.2, Self-Consistency 44.6, ReAct 47.6, CRITIC w/o Tool 42.0, CRITIC 50.0. Some math-program rows show w/o Tool 68.3 (-1.8) vs CRITIC 72.2 (+2.1) on one dataset.
limits: Pdf text extraction scrambled column labels, so per-dataset assignment of some cells is uncertain; the direction (tool beats no-tool; no-tool at or below CoT on QA) is clear. Tasks are QA, program-of-thought math, toxicity.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 mostly closed for the self-edit case: an external verifier explains most of the edit gain. It does not test whether a retrieved example adds value beyond the verifier, because no retrieved case is used.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching LLMs to self-debug
finding: Editing a failed program using execution feedback is far more sample efficient than drawing more fresh samples. One debug turn is usually enough.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL: debugging from greedy decoding matched baseline with 16 samples; debugging from 8 samples beat baseline with 32 samples. Abstract: matches or beats baselines that generate more than 10x candidates. Accuracy gain from further turns after the first is within 0.1%.
limits: Code only. Codex / GPT-class models of 2023. Feedback comes from an executor and unit tests or a self-written code explanation; cost of the explanation tokens is not counted in the 16-sample comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 evidence for code only: edit-with-execution beats fresh sampling at roughly equal or lower sample count. Still no reasoning-task equivalent without a verifier.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-Debugging, feedback-type ablations
finding: Unit-test feedback helps on every set. A model-written code explanation adds a smaller gain on top and is the only feedback available when no tests exist. The no-test case is a 2 to 3 point gain on Spider.
numbers: Spider: Codex baseline 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation feedback (no tests). Abstract: 2 to 3% on Spider, 9% on the hardest level, up to 12% on TransCoder/MBPP with tests. MBPP table: baseline 61.4 up to 70.8 with test+explanation (read from a table with scrambled labels).
limits: Explanation-only gain is the intrinsic-feedback case and is small; test-based gain is the large part. Code domain.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a separate explain-then-edit step gives a few points where there is no verifier, much more with one. Supports spending on tests first, diagnosis second.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: Survey finds no prior work shows successful self-correction with prompted-LLM feedback, outside tasks specially suited to it. Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale finetuning enables it. Many positive results used oracle information or weak initial prompts.
numbers: Qualitative survey; no pooled effect size given.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Review of a literature that stops mid-2024. Does not test retrieved-case editing.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: independent confirmation (second review beside Huang) that the verifier is what gives the gain. Our edit step must always be gated by an external check.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe)
finding: Measured how often a model's second attempt turns a correct first answer wrong. Prompted base and Self-Refine often break correct answers; SFT-style training reduces but does not remove it.
numbers: MATH, Gemini 1.5 Flash: base accuracy at turn 1 52.6, turn 2 41.4 (-11.2); correct-to-incorrect 15.8%, incorrect-to-correct 4.6%. Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8; c-to-i 4.2%, i-to-c 3.2%. STaR 53.6 to 54.0; Pair-SFT 52.4 to 54.2. SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4, c-to-i 1.4%.
limits: Edit of own answer with a generic 'there may be an error' prompt, no retrieved case, no external check. Gemini family. Fractions are of all problems, not only the initially correct ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: a measured break rate of 4.2% to 15.8% of all items for blind prompted editing on MATH. The retrieved-case rate is still unknown, but our edit step needs a keep-original-if-not-verified rule.

source: Zhang et al. (2024/2025) Understanding the dark side of LLMs' intrinsic self-correction
finding: Intrinsic self-correction makes models waver and overturn correct answers, including in recent models. Answers change often across a 10-round chat.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B: accuracy drop 20.4 points with 58.8% of correct answers overturned. GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of final answers more than 6 times in 10 rounds. Inner answers change 14.1% vs 8.3% at initial generation (Llama).
limits: Prompts like 'Are you sure?'; tasks are simple factual QA plus complex tasks; models include ChatGPT, Llama, DeepSeek families. No retrieved case.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: more measured break rates, up to 58.8% overturned for a small model under a doubt prompt. Confirms that a doubt-style edit step is dangerous. A retrieved case may change this; untested.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Compared two memory units: abstracted insights vs retrieved successful trajectories, plus both. Which unit wins depends on the task: insights help reasoning-over-text (HotpotQA), raw trajectories help action-heavy tasks (ALFWorld). Both together beat either alone.
numbers: Insights-only / retrieve-only success rate: HotpotQA 36% / 31%; ALFWorld 50% / 55%; WebShop 37% / 38% (score 0.675 / 0.67). Full ExpeL beats both. Insights extracted from the few-shot examples alone gave no gain over ReAct.
limits: gpt-3.5 agents, three environments, small N per cell. Insights are distilled from success-failure pairs, not edit rules. ExpeL does not run a case-edit step.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed with a direct head-to-head: no single best unit. Abstract rules for reasoning, concrete cases for action. Implement both and let the task type decide; the tie on WebShop suggests the unit matters less than having experience at all.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL, ablation on how in-context trajectories are selected
finding: Selecting examples by task similarity beat selecting by reasoning-step similarity, which beat random choice. Random selection gave a significant drop.
numbers: Table 3 lower block: task-similarity retrieval best; reasoning-similarity noticeably lower; random sampled a large drop. Cell values are scrambled in the extracted text so exact numbers are not recorded.
limits: Compares similarity measures, not editability. No adaptation-guided variant. gpt-3.5 agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 still open for editable selection; this only shows task-level similarity is a sound default over random for action tasks.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: Memory of strategies and code, curated and rewritten by the model, beats both raw-history appending and raw-example retrieval. Gains are large for some models and tasks and tiny or negative for others. Part of the gain comes from a stronger plain prompt with no memory.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet / GPT-4o. AIME 2024: BL 23.3 / 20.0; DC- (no memory, strong prompt) 36.7 / 36.7; Dynamic Retrieval (raw similar pairs) 43.3 / 26.7; DC-Cu 50.0 / 36.7; DC-RS 46.7 / 40.0. Game of 24 GPT-4o: BL 10, DR 6, DC-Cu 93, DC-RS 99. GPQA Diamond Sonnet: BL 59.6, DR 63.6, DC-RS 68.7; GPT-4o 57.1 to 57.1. MMLU-Pro Eng GPT-4o: BL 53.2, DR 48.8, DC-RS 51.2. Full-history append on AIME 2024: Sonnet 26.7, GPT-4o 6.7 (BL 20.0).
limits: Small test sets (AIME 30 questions per year). Game of 24 jump is a code-reuse effect (memory stores a Python solver). No equal-token control; DC adds memory text tokens. Single paper, early 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4, 6, 7: (4) a curated abstract memory beat raw retrieved examples; (6) gains persist on a strong model for some tasks but vanish for GPT-4o on GPQA; (7) raw retrieved cases lowered GPT-4o below baseline on Game of 24 (10 to 6) and MMLU-Pro Eng (53.2 to 48.8). Always test against a strong no-memory prompt (DC-).

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, retrieval confusion note
finding: Authors state that for GPT-4o retrieval can add confusion when suboptimal examples are recalled, and that uncurated history can hurt.
numbers: GPT-4o AIME 2024: baseline 20.0, full-history 6.7, DC-RS 40.0.
quote: retrieval can, in some cases, introduce confusion, especially if suboptimal examples are recalled
limits: Qualitative explanation from the authors' output review, not a controlled test of cause.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: direct report of negative transfer from retrieved cases for a strong model. Add a relevance check or abstraction step before showing a case to the editor.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/2026) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Distilled strategy-level memory items (from successes and failures) beat trajectory memory (Synapse) and workflow memory (AWM) on WebArena, and raw trajectories do not generalise to the cross-site split.
numbers: WebArena overall SR, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5, Synapse 42.1, AWM 44.1, ReasoningBank 48.8, with MaTTS scaling 51.8. Multi-site split: no memory 10.3, AWM 3.4 (worse), ReasoningBank 13.8, +MaTTS 17.2. Up to 20% relative gain and 16% fewer steps claimed.
limits: Web navigation; an LLM judge labels success so memory can be wrong. Distillation prompts differ across baselines. Not edit of a retrieved case but strategy lookup.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: head-to-head of trajectory vs workflow vs distilled-reasoning units. Abstract reasoning items win; workflows can hurt on cross-site transfer. Supports O7 memory unit = short distilled item, not whole solution.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/2026) ReasoningBank, failure ablation
finding: Adding failed trajectories to the memory builder helped ReasoningBank but not the baselines, which only store successes and flatline or drop when failures are added. This is the closest measured LLM test of CHEF-style learning from failures.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: success-only vs with-failures: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2, ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7.
limits: Failure lessons are written after the fact and retrieved by task similarity; they do not anticipate failures before planning as CHEF does. One domain slice for this ablation; no seeds reported in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: failure-derived lessons add about 3 points when distilled well, and hurt when stored as raw trajectories. CHEF-style pre-emptive prediction by failure index is still untested.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with LLMs
finding: Retrieving a high-level thought template and instantiating it per problem beats single-query and multi-query prompting at about 12% of the cost of multi-query methods.
numbers: Abstract: over previous SOTA, +11% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One; cost about 12% of multi-query methods such as tree of thoughts. Table row: Game of 24 GPT-4 3.0 vs BoT 82.4.
limits: Template instantiation is a form of case adaptation with abstracted cases. Reported by the authors, GPT-4 era. No ablation against a whole-solution memory.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 1: abstract templates reach high gains at low token cost on reasoning tasks, a token-fair win over multi-query search. Not tested against best-of-N at equal tokens.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage rises log-linearly with the number of fresh samples, so a best-of-N fresh baseline is strong where an automatic verifier exists. Any edit method must beat it at equal tokens.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% solved with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples, beating the single-sample state of the art.
limits: Needs a verifier for selection; on tasks without one, majority voting and reward models plateau. Cost at 250 samples is large.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: sets the bar. Compare edit-one-retrieved-case at equal tokens against N fresh samples with the same verifier; no paper has done it on a reasoning task.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) CBR-DDI: case-based reasoning enhances LLMs on drug-drug interaction
finding: Retrieval of similar cases alone brings most of the gain over the bare LLM; adding case refinement and knowledge paths adds a further 16 to 23 points. The gain holds for a 671B model. In the familiar-drug setting (S0) fine-tuned baselines do better.
numbers: Accuracy column: Llama3.1-8B base 8.71, Naive-CBR 47.88, CBR-DDI 68.52; Llama3.1-70B base 8.93, Naive-CBR 48.09, CBR-DDI 71.36; DeepSeek-V3 base 12.62, Naive-CBR 55.20, CBR-DDI 71.05. Abstract: +28.7% over popular LLMs and CBR baseline; base beaten by 463%.
quote: Under the S0 setting, existing methods can memorize possible interaction types between known drugs
limits: Biomedical link prediction, base accuracy very low so room is large. The adaptation part is bundled with KG paths and a sampling strategy, so the pure edit effect is not isolated. Column mapping read from a scrambled table.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6: (6) the gain of the CBR pipeline over Naive-CBR does not shrink from 8B to 671B (20.6 / 23.3 / 15.9 points). (5) authors state fine-tuned models win when query drugs were seen (S0), echoing Ye et al.: a plain model wins on familiar queries.

source: Wilkerson and Leake (2024) On implementing case-based reasoning with large language models (ICCBR 2024); Leake and Ye (2021) Harmonizing case retrieval and adaptation with alternating optimization (ICCBR 2021)
finding: Both papers located by DOI (Crossref, Semantic Scholar: 25 and 10 citations) but full text and abstracts are closed access. Not read. No numbers can be recorded.
numbers: none read
limits: Springer returns an HTML paywall page for the PDF. The open-access route needs an email address for Unpaywall, which was not sent. DOI of Leake-Ye: 10.1007/978-3-030-86957-1_9.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. K05 (retrieval and adaptation out of step) rests only on Ye et al. numbers; nothing new to change it.

source: Smyth and Keane (1998) Adaptation-guided retrieval: questioning the similarity assumption in reasoning (Artificial Intelligence 102)
finding: Located by DOI via Crossref; ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403, so the Deja Vu results were not read. Companion 1995 paper 'Experiments on adaptation-guided retrieval in case-based design' (DOI 10.1007/3-540-60598-3_28) also paywalled.
numbers: none read

agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for both the classic numbers and any LLM test. Keep K18 single-source, unread.
